entities.summary:
ETH Zurich (Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule Zürich — Swiss Federal Institute of Technology), founded in 1855 by the Swiss Confederation, is Europe's leading science and technology university — producing 21 Nobel laureates and alumni including Albert Einstein, Wilhelm Röntgen, and Nils Bohr. Einstein completed his physics degree at ETH in 1900 and returned as a professor in 1912; the Annalen der Physik submission containing his 1905 special relativity paper was drafted while he was a clerk at the Bern patent office trying to escape ETH's rejection of his graduate application.

The Swiss Confederation established ETH as a national engineering and science institution to accelerate Swiss industrialization — building on Switzerland's watchmaking, textile, and chemical manufacturing base. ETH's Location in Zurich gave it access to Switzerland's banking, pharmaceutical, and precision engineering industries. The main building on Rämistrasse, designed by Gottfried Semper (also designer of Vienna's natural history museum), looks down over the old town from its hill.

ETH Zurich's research legacy spans relativity (Einstein), X-rays (Röntgen studied here), the World Wide Web prototype (Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN nearby), chemistry (Linus Pauling's collaborator Robert Huber), and materials science. The ETH domain includes EMPA (materials), PSI (particle physics), Eawag (water research), and WSL (forest and landscape ecology) — creating an integrated Swiss science ecosystem. Switzerland's per-capita Nobel Prize rate (highest in the world for natural sciences) depends substantially on ETH research productivity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: ETH Zurich's most consequential contribution — Einstein's formation and return — connected the institution to the development of special relativity, the most transformative scientific theory of the 20th century.
